answer: The relation between socioeconomic status and the chance of BA degree completion is affected by the individual's race: race significantly moderates the SES–degree-completion association, such that the per-SD-SES increase in the odds of completing a BA is much stronger for Black respondents (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.47–2.90) and directionally stronger for Hispanic respondents (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.12–2.46) than for White respondents (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.02–1.36). A joint test of the two SES x race interactions is significant (Wald chi2(2)=8.87, p=0.003; LR chi2(2)=9.63, p=0.008), driven primarily by the SES_x_Black term (interaction OR 1.76, p=0.003; SES_x_Hispanic OR 1.41, p=0.110). Predicted probabilities confirm that the racial gap is largest at low SES and narrows at higher SES — e.g., at SES_z=-1/0/+1, White 3.20/3.74/4.37%, Black 0.71/1.46/2.97%, Hispanic 1.13/1.85/3.03% — yet White respondents retain a higher completion probability at every SES level. Results are robust to separate per-race models, Firth penalized estimation (no separation), bootstrap CIs (Black SES OR [1.43-2.88]), and non-linearity checks (SES^2 n.s., p=0.53), and the Black interaction persists even after adjusting for academic resources (mediators). Caveats: the interaction is a multiplicative/odds-scale effect within uniformly low completion rates (2.7%; only 28 Black and 19 Hispanic completers) so minority estimates carry wide CIs; adding FAMILY SIZE as a covariate attenuates the interaction (joint p=0.19) indicating specification sensitivity (family size is a socioeconomic-background component); analysis is unweighted and associative, not causal.

payload.hypothesis: The relation between socioeconomic status and the chance of BA degree completion is affected by race: the SES gradient in the odds of completing a BA is significantly steeper for Black (OR 2.07 per SD SES) and directionally steeper for Hispanic (OR 1.66) than for White respondents (OR 1.18), with a significant joint SES x race interaction (chi2(2)=8.9, p=0.003); the race gap is largest at low SES and narrows, but never closes, at higher SES, and White respondents retain a higher completion probability at every SES level.
payload.workflow: Logistic moderation analysis: P(BA=1) = logit^-1(b0 + b1*SES_z + b2*Black + b3*Hispanic + b4*SES_z*Black + b5*SES_z*Hispanic + b6*Male) on all 8,773 NLS respondents (236 BA completers), SES z-standardized, White reference. Headline test: joint Wald (chi2(2)=8.87, p=0.0029) and LR (chi2(2)=9.63, p=0.0081) of the two interactions. Reporting: per-race SES ORs with delta-method CIs, predicted probabilities at SES_z=-1,0,+1. Robustness: separate per-race models, Firth penalized logit (no separation), non-linearity (SES^2) diagnostic, family-size sensitivity, mediator direct-effect model (+ASVAB, +class percentile), and 500-iteration bootstrap percentile CIs.
